items.title: The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles-Elimination Status. Here’s What That Means
items.standfirst: After more than a year of continuous measles transmission, the U.S. has lost a public-health milestone it held for more than two decades.
items.content: For more than a quarter of a century, the U.S. has held measles-elimination status, meaning the virus was no longer spreading continuously within the country. Prior to the introduction of the first measles vaccine in 1963, nearly all American children contracted the disease before they were 15, for an annual case count of up to four million, including 400 to 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations. But an aggressive vaccination campaign changed all of that, and measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000. No more.On Nov. 17, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced that the U.S. had lost that status after at least 12 months of uninterrupted transmission. Falling vaccination rates—fueled in part by antivaccine misinformation spread by a vocal community that includes Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)—have allowed the virus, contained for more than a generation, to spread widely. As of Nov. 12, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) had recorded 5,412 measles cases in the U.S. in 2026: 5,394 reported by 47 jurisdictions, plus 18 cases among international visitors. That case count is more than twice the 2,289 cases reported in all of 2025, including three deaths—the highest caseload since 1991—and is 19 times greater than the 285 cases in 2024.“It's a tremendous step backwards for public health in the United States,” says Dr. Paul Offit, attending physician in the Division of Infectious Diseases at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. “But, in some ways, the ruling is irrelevant. Measles has now established a foothold in this country. It's endemic.”As with so much else in the field of epidemiology, the standards that must be met to gain or lose elimination status for measles aren't entirely straightforward. For one thing, elimination doesn’t mean zero cases. Measles can still be brought into the country by travelers and spread among people who aren’t protected.Even cases that appear to have a domestic origin are not necessarily enough to cost a country its elimination status. PAHO considers measles transmission re-established when the same virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted in a country for at least 12 months. In the U.S., the outbreak began on Jan. 20, 2025, and reached that threshold a year later, according to PAHO. Genome sequencing helps scientists identify the genotype and lineage of the virus in a case and determine whether it is linked to an ongoing chain of transmission. In August, Utah health officials published a preprint study documenting sustained transmission in the state. The PAHO commission reviewed the evidence from across the country before determining that the U.S. had lost its elimination status. In 2026 so far, the CDC has reported 43 new outbreaks nationwide, nearly matching the 48 reported in all of 2025.Vaccination rates don’t have to fall much for outbreaks to take hold, especially in communities with pockets of low coverage. PAHO says communities should aim for at least 95% coverage with both doses of the measles vaccine to help prevent transmission. High vaccination coverage also helps protect people who can’t be vaccinated, including infants too young to receive the vaccine and people with certain medical conditions. MMR vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026, according to the CDC.“It’s so tragic that we’ve allowed measles to return to America,” says Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of Texas Children’s Hospital Center for Vaccine Development. “In the prevaccine era, measles exhibited a distinctive seasonality in late winter [and] early spring. This same pattern has recurred in 2025 and 2026, so the prediction is we will [see] an even larger surge at that time in 2027.”What makes things worse is that while measles is an easy illness to prevent—two doses of the MMR vaccine reduce the risk of contracting the disease by 97%—it is wildly easy to catch and spread. An unvaccinated person who comes into contact with someone with measles has a 90% chance of becoming infected, according to Johns Hopkins Medicine, and the virus can linger on surfaces or in the air for up to two hours after an infected person has left a room. What’s more, people who are infected with the virus can be stealth carriers before they even know they’re sick. According to the World Health Organization, the virus can spread for up to four days before the disease’s characteristic rash appears and four more days after it has faded.And the disease can lead to serious, sometimes fatal complications. “Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, at a Nov. 17 press conference. “It can cause pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness, and even death.”The U.S. is not alone in battling a measles resurgence; the problem extends across the Americas. In Nov. 2025, Canada lost its elimination status following an outbreak that began in Oct. 2024, spread across 10 provinces and the Northwest Territories, and lasted more than a year. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their elimination status on Nov. 17. In these countries, as in the U.S., gaps in vaccination coverage have helped fuel outbreaks.Regaining America’s lost measles-elimination status won’t be easy. Kennedy’s continued questioning of public-health authorities could complicate efforts to rebuild trust in vaccination. In August, he went so far as to speculate, in a post on X, that the announcement by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro of two measles-related deaths in the state “may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers.”Regaining elimination status will require interrupting endemic transmission for at least 12 months, documenting that progress, and strengthening vaccination, surveillance, and outbreak response.“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” Barbosa said at the Nov. 17 press conference. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day.”Adds Offit: “We will be dealing with measles this year and next year and the year after that, until we get our immunization rates up.”

items.title: The Democrats Who Voted Against Nominating Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker of the House
items.standfirst: While the ballots were cast in secret, several newly-elected Democrats have confirmed that they voted against Jeffries' nomination.
items.content: Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York secured the vast majority of House Democrats’ support in his nomination for Speaker of the House. Eleven members of his party, however, voted against giving him the nod.The ballots were cast in secret, so the identities of some of the Democrats who cast “no” votes are not yet known. But seven progressive members-elect—Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, and Claire Valdez of New York—issued a joint statement on Wednesday, in which they revealed that they opposed Jeffries for the role.“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the members-elect said in their statement. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”“While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they continued. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”A spokesperson for Haynes released a statement on Wednesday saying that the Congressman-elect “woke up unexpectedly ill” that morning and had missed the vote, meaning that he was not among the 11 members who voted against nominating Jeffries. The spokesperson said, though, that Haynes had intended to vote no, per the joint statement. Haynes previously spoke highly of Jeffries in an interview with TIME. “There are some people when you meet them and they’re young, you know they have the ‘it’ factor,” the member-elect said to TIME. “You know that they are hungry for knowledge. They are determined to make a difference.”Five of the incoming lawmakers who signed onto the joint statement—Chevalier, Kiros, McKinney, Rabb, and Valdez—are Democratic socialists. Another progressive member-elect, Don Leonard of Ohio, confirmed in a story posted on his Instagram account that he had voted against Jeffries’ nomination. Last week, Leonard shared a video on his social media account, in which he claimed that senior members of the party told him his life would become a “living hell” if he didn’t back Jeffries.In an interview with CNN that aired on Sunday, Leonard said that he had met with Jeffries. He shared some of the issues he wanted the New York lawmaker to address, including tackling corruption and “call the question on U.S. aid to Israel.”“What I tried to impress upon Leader Jeffries is what we need in this moment right now is not just a caucus leader, but a leader of the Democratic Party,” Leonard told CNN. “And that what I was seeing from the letter that he requested my support for his speakership was not indicative of the kind of things that my constituents need to see in order to put our faith that he is able to lead us.”Newly-elected Angela Gonzales-Torres of California, a Democratic socialist, revealed on social media on Wednesday afternoon that she also voted “no.”“Voters gave us a chance on November 3rd to actually make a difference in their lives. A chance to deliver on affordable housing. A chance to deliver Medicare for All. A chance to abolish ICE and hold the corrupt elite accountable,” she said. “Since day one, I have been telling leadership that Angelenos have not been satisfied with the status quo and are demanding transformative change. I voted NO today, keeping my community and the trust they instilled in me in mind.”The other three members who voted against Jeffries’ nomination are unknown at this time.Despite the opposition of the few holdouts, the vote on Wednesday was an overwhelming 251-11, allowing Jeffries’ nomination to sail through. No one challenged the New York lawmaker for the nomination.The official House vote to elect the Speaker, as well as other leaders in the chamber, will take place on Jan. 3.The backing of the House Democratic caucus, which will hold a significant majority in the next Congress, all but assures that Jeffries will win the position on the lower chamber’s floor and become the first Black American to hold the role of Speaker of the House.When asked about his detractors during a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, Jeffries replied, “The results of today’s election speak for themselves,” adding that “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other.” He went on to say that it’s “an honor to be serving with a majority” in the House, with members “from all across the country” and that the party was embracing “people who have different perspectives.”“We’re going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people,” Jeffries said. “That’s our commitment. And the overwhelming majority of people within the caucus have spoken.”

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries Easily Wins Caucus Vote to Be Next Speaker of the House
items.standfirst: Jeffries faced no challenger and secured the nomination in a 251-11 vote
items.content: House Democrats nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York for Speaker on Wednesday, putting him one step closer to becoming the first Black American to lead the chamber after steering his party to a sweeping victory in this month's midterm elections.Jeffries, 56, faced no challenger in the closed-door election and secured the nomination in a 251 to 11 vote. The ballots were cast secretly through an application on lawmakers' phones, leaving the identities of those who opposed him undisclosed unless they chose to make their votes public.The vote marked a milestone in Jeffries's political career, four years after he succeeded Nancy Pelosi as the top House Democrat and more than a decade after he entered Congress. Now, he is preparing to take charge of a chamber where Democrats are projected to hold 259 seats, a commanding majority that would give him considerably more room to maneuver than the narrow Republican majority that preceded it.Immediately after the vote, seven incoming progressive Democrats confirmed they had voted against Jeffries, including Representatives-elect Claire Valdez of New York, Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania. (Representative-Elect Frederick Haynes of Texas was also on the list, but did not make it to the vote because he woke up feeling unwell, his office said.) They said in a joint statement that they had been negotiating with Jeffries over the party’s agenda and had made progress, but were not yet satisfied with the commitments they had received. "Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the lawmakers said. "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."The defections did little to dismiss what was an otherwise decisive show of support for Jeffries, whose nomination was put forward by Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, Mark Pocan of Wisconsin, Derek Tran of California, Rebecca Bennett of New Jersey, and Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. He will serve alongside Representatives Ted Lieu of California as Democratic caucus chair, Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, and Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip. The full House will vote to formally elect its leaders when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3.The transition from minority leader to Speaker will put Jeffries at the center of the political battles during the final two years of President Trump's term, giving Democrats control over the House's legislative agenda and investigative committees. His party has promised to use that authority to scrutinize the Trump Administration and demonstrate to voters that Democrats can govern ahead of the 2028 presidential election.Read more: In Hakeem Jeffries’ Rise to Speaker, Black Leaders See a Milestone—and a Test“Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one,” Jeffries said at a news conference following the leadership vote. “We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you.”Wednesday's vote was conducted by secret ballot, a decision Jeffries announced Tuesday after some of his allies had favored nominating him by acclamation, without a formal tally. The recorded vote was intended to allow lawmakers to register their views privately, with the results revealing the level of support for Jeffries but not how individual members voted.For some of the party's most senior members, the proceedings were an occasion to reflect on the historical significance of Jeffries's ascent. "This is a very surreal moment for me," Clyburn, a longtime South Carolina Democrat and former member of the House leadership, told reporters before entering the room. "And when it comes my turn to second his nomination, I'm going to be thinking about John, Lillian, and Emily,” he said, referring to the late John Lewis, an influential civil rights activist and congressman.Representative Steny Hoyer of Maryland, who served for years alongside Pelosi and Clyburn in the party's previous leadership team, recalled witnessing the election of the first woman to become speaker. "It's a historic time," Hoyer said as he entered the room. "I've now served here for the first woman who was elected speaker of the House, and now we're going to see the first African American. I think it's a testimony to the progress that we've made in America."Pushback from progressives The nomination followed an extensive effort by Jeffries and his allies to consolidate support in the days since the election. They solicited endorsements from major Democratic factions, contacted lawmakers who had expressed reservations and sought to meet with members of the large incoming class before Wednesday's vote. Jeffries personally met with leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, and the Blue Dog Coalition.The push came amid a campaign by progressive activists to persuade Democrats to reject Jeffries, whom some critics regard as too closely aligned with corporate interests and insufficiently willing to challenge the party's establishment. Congressional offices were inundated with calls and emails, and an online petition seeking an alternative candidate attracted more than a million signatures.At a Democratic conference in Denver over the weekend, protesters repeatedly interrupted Jeffries with demands for Medicare for All, a Green New Deal, and an embargo on American weapons transfers to Israel. Some protesters also gathered Wednesday outside the room where Democrats were voting on leadership.Progressive lawmakers have pressed Jeffries to promise a committee markup next year on Medicare for All legislation and bring forward the Block the Bombs Act, which would restrict certain offensive weapons transfers to Israel. Asked on Wednesday if he would move towards the progressive left on these issues, Jeffries declined to commit. “We're going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people,” he said.The public pressure from progressives did not translate into an organized challenge inside the House Democratic caucus as it did in the upper chamber, where Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has launched a bid to replace Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader, over similar frustrations with the party's leadership. Though Schumer appears likely to retain his leadership post, Senate Democrats aren’t expected to settle that contest until next month.In the House, prominent Democrats whose names circulated as possible alternatives to Jeffries declined to run. Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland ruled out a bid as he’s in line to chair the powerful House Judiciary Committee, while Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, the subject of an online effort to draft her, made clear that she did not want the position. "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people," Pressley told constituents at a town hall on Monday.Jeffries’ path to the gavelMinutes after his selection as the Speaker-designate, Jeffries posted a childhood photograph of himself on social media and quoted his favorite rapper, the Notorious B.I.G. “Stay far from timid, only make moves when your heart’s in it and live the phrase Sky’s the Limit,” the caption read.Now on the doorstep of history, Jeffries reflected on how far he had come from his upbringing in Brooklyn, where he grew up as the son of an Air Force veteran and a social worker. “I was raised in a working-class neighborhood in Crown Heights,” he said at Wednesday’s news conference. “During the first 12 years of my life, my congresswoman—though I never met her—was Shirley Chisholm, a trailblazer extraordinaire. And part of the journey that all of us are on is that we recognize we stand on the shoulders of so many giants, and that young man was someone who was being so effectively represented by Shirley Chisholm, and now he has an opportunity…to try to do the same for the children of America for such a time as this.”Jeffries often recalls how the devastation of the crack epidemic during the 1980s shaped his interest in public service and his desire to improve conditions for working-class families who remained in struggling neighborhoods. After attending the State University of New York at Binghamton, Georgetown University and New York University School of Law, Jeffries worked as a corporate lawyer before turning to politics. He lost his first two campaigns for the New York State Assembly, but he eventually won a seat in the Legislature. In 2012, he challenged a longtime Democratic congressman who withdrew from the race, clearing a path for his election to the House.Read more: Jeffries' Fraternity Days Set Stage For His CareerIn Congress, Jeffries has developed a reputation as a disciplined political communicator and coalition builder, cultivating relationships across the party's ideological spectrum as he rose through its leadership ranks. When Pelosi stepped aside after the 2022 elections, he succeeded her as the top House Democrat, becoming the first Black lawmaker to lead either party in Congress.Representative Steven Horsford of Nevada, the former chair of the Congressional Black Caucus and a close friend of Jeffries, called him a “consensus builder” and "listener.”“I came in with Speaker-to-be Jeffries as a freshman,” Horsford said. “He's about building coalition. Yes, we're a diverse party. We have different viewpoints, but in the end, we're here for one common goal, and that is to deliver for the American people.”Representative Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is also Black, credited Jeffries for the party's resounding wins in the midterms. "It was his strategy to pick good candidates, to fund good candidates, to give us the ability to reform our government the way the American people spoke clearly," Carter said. "Hakeem Jeffries has been the architect of that."Jeffries' election as speaker would carry a historic significance beyond his own career, placing a Black American for the first time in an office second in the line of presidential succession, after the Vice President. It would also come more than 150 years after Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black member of the House during Reconstruction.“America is a great country, but not a perfect country,” Jeffries said Wednesday. “But the framers of this democracy gave every generation the ability to work hard, to show up, to speak up, stand up, and help the country march toward a more perfect union. And that's what House Democrats at this moment represent: people from all walks of life, different corners of the country, who are here in order to make a difference in the lives of the American people.”Debate over working with RepublicansDemocrats have promised to use their control of Congress to pursue an ambitious legislative agenda and subject the Trump Administration to the kind of scrutiny that Republican leaders have largely resisted. The House's investigative committees would be able to examine allegations of corruption and abuses of executive authority, as well as the administration's handling of the war in Iran. Some Democrats are openly discussing impeachment proceedings against senior administration officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.But their ability to enact legislation will remain constrained by Trump's veto power and the Senate's 60-vote threshold for advancing most bills. Those obstacles have helped fuel a debate over whether the party should concentrate on legislation that might attract Republican support or pursue more ambitious measures that could establish its priorities for the 2028 election.Jeffries has sought to leave room for both approaches, outlining an agenda organized around affordability and accountability. His immediate priorities include restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired earlier this year, reversing Republican Medicaid spending cuts, and repealing tariffs imposed by the Trump Administration.Less than 24 hours before the nomination vote, Jeffries held a news conference and laid out more of his legislative vision. He embraced proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing benefits, and guarantee health coverage for children. "Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage," Jeffries told reporters.The proposals drew praise from Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, the leading proponent of Medicare for All, who said they resembled the first stage of his plan to move the country toward a single-payer system. But Jeffries has stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All itself, a distinction that illustrates the policy disagreements he will encounter even on an issue that Democrats have identified as a central priority.The Congressional Progressive Caucus is expected to grow to more than 100 members in the next Congress, while the New Democrat Coalition, the largest ideological faction in the House Democratic Caucus, will number more than 140. Both groups support expanding access to health care and reversing Republican cuts, but they differ over whether Democrats should seek to replace the existing insurance system. The New Democrats have expressed skepticism about Medicare for All, arguing that competition among private insurers can help control costs. Progressives are also seeking more aggressive action on corporate power, campaign finance, and American military assistance to Israel, among other issues. Their growing ranks could give them substantial influence over the House agenda, even if their efforts to challenge Jeffries's leadership gained little traction.The political circumstances are almost the reverse of those confronting Pelosi when Democrats last reclaimed the House during a Trump presidency. In 2018, it was moderate Democrats who objected to her return as speaker, arguing that the party needed new leadership after years under her command. Pelosi ultimately overcame the resistance and went on to wield considerable authority over Trump's first term, overseeing major investigations and two impeachments of the President. Jeffries now faces skepticism primarily from the left, though he approaches the speakership with a larger majority and without the organized challenge that confronted his predecessor. Representative-elect Don Leonard of Ohio said in a video posted to social media last week that senior Democrats had warned him they would make his life a "living hell" if he refused to support Jeffries. Leonard posted a picture of his ballot on Wednesday afternoon, showing that he was one of the 11 Democrats voting against Jeffries.Still, Jeffries's allies dismissed suggestions that the dissent could substantially weaken his authority. "Given the size of our majority that we won by, you know, I don't think any of the pressures some people think he's going to face are going to be an issue," Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a centrist Democrat, told reporters Wednesday.Asked if he feels the need to negotiate with the 11 lawmakers who defected, Jeffries responded bluntly: “The results of today's election speak for themselves. We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other.”Hakeem Jeffries Easily Wins Caucus Vote to Be Next U.S. Speaker of the House

items.title: Mary Peltola Defeats Incumbent Republican in Alaska Senate Race
items.standfirst: Democratic challenger Mary Peltola triumphed over Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, rounding out a controversy-plagued race and handing the Democratic caucus a 56-44 majority in the Senate.
items.content: Mary Peltola speaks during a midterm election night party in Anchorage, Alaska, on Nov. 3, 2026. —Charly Triballeau—Getty ImagesDemocratic challenger Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska, rounding out one of the tightest and most controversial races of the midterm elections, and marking another notable GOP loss in what is typically a reliably red state.The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday evening, two weeks after Election Day, with Peltola securing 50.1% of the votes against Sullivan’s 45.8%. Peltola is the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Alaska since 2008. Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election.Peltola, a Yup'ik Alaska Native, served one term in the House of Representatives from 2022 to 2025 and became the first Alaska Native member of Congress and the first woman to represent Alaska in the lower chamber. She’ll now be the first Alaska Native in the Senate.Read More: The Candidates Who Made History in the MidtermsThe Alaska race is the last U.S. Senate contest to be called, partly due to the razor-thin margin between Peltola and Sullivan, but also because Alaska has a 15-day grace period after Election Day for mailed ballots to be returned to the elections office and counted. The state uses a ranked-choice voting system, which can make the process of certifying votes more complicated and would have resulted in a second round of vote tabulating if the leading candidate had received less than 50% of the first-round votes cast.Peltola posted on social media following the election call that “there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first. Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”Her victory puts the Senate balance of power at 56-44, in favor of Democrats, who secured control of both chambers of Congress in the midterms as the American public appeared to reject President Donald Trump amid concerns about the Iran war, inflation, and more. In the eight Senate contests that appeared least predictable, Democrats won all of them, and they even won in Mississippi too, where election forecasters had rated the race as likely Republican.Read More: The Democratic Wins No Election Forecaster ExpectedThe race was dominated by controversy over allegations that independent runner Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, was a spoiler candidate, intended to confuse Alaskans and draw votes away from the incumbent Republican Senator with the same first and last name.Despite protests from Trump, Republicans were unsuccessful in trying to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot. A federal judge on Nov. 1 dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump Administration that sought to delay certifying the results in Alaska if the incumbent Republican lost the race. "The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” ruled District Judge Sharon Gleason, referring to the Oct. 22 lawsuit. The New York Times on Oct. 28 reported that “operatives” aligned with Peltola had “spent months recruiting candidates to peel votes from Senator Dan Sullivan.” Peltola vehemently denied the claims.Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, launched a probe into the matter on Oct. 29, to investigate what he alleged to be an “organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.” On Election Day, Sen. Sullivan said “people are disgusted by what has gone down in Alaska” and alleged that America was “witnessing the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska.” Peltola described the noise around the double Sullivan controversy as “just another distraction,” dismissing it as “stuff to sell newspapers, stuff to get subscriptions.”Amid the fallout, Peltola’s campaign sued Alaska in an effort to obtain the records on rejected absentee ballots. The lawsuit, filed Nov. 6, argued the failure to release the records would amount to “severely prejudicing [Peltola’s] ability to monitor Alaska’s election certification process to make sure that all ballots are counted according to law.” Alaska Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled against the campaign’s request on Nov. 11, stipulating that the records “cannot reasonably be produced at this juncture, nor redacted of confidential information.”Trump, meanwhile, accused Peltola of “perpetrating such a terrible scheme” and argued that incumbent Sen. Sullivan should be prematurely announced as winner, even as Peltola inched slightly ahead in the counted votes. In a Truth Social post on Nov. 5, Trump said that the votes for Dan J. Sullivan, as well as those for Gerald Heikes, a GOP runner and the fourth candidate on Alaska’s ballot, should be “given to the REAL Dan Sullivan” insisting there is “no other fair solution.” Trump doubled down on his argument on Nov. 7, claiming that if all those votes were combined, then the Alaska race would be “over” and the incumbent Senator would be announced as the winner.Aside from the controversy which dominated much of the discourse around the race, Peltola and Sullivan also clashed over proposals to build data centers in Alaska, an issue felt nationwide.When asked about data centers, Peltola said she takes her “cue from the people of that region,” deferring to local support, provided it doesn’t strain the grid for existing ratepayers. Whereas Sullivan has pushed to bring data centers onto Alaska’s Air Force and joint military installations.Peltola also hit out at Sullivan for continuing to support Trump’s war with Iran, which remains deeply unpopular with Americans, in part due to the financial ramifications of the conflict which has entered its ninth month. The disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade route, has led to record high diesel prices.In an NBC exit poll carried out Nov. 3, more than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities including gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.

items.title: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a 56-seat Senate majority
items.standfirst: It's the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state.
items.content: Former Rep. Mary Peltola ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska — the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state.Her win gives Democrats a 56-44 edge in the Senate.Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration.Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House.Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots.But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent.The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. Both had previously denied involvement.

items.title: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.standfirst: Several moderate Democrats have already placed calls to the White House and Trump administration officials to express a willingness to work together.
items.content: In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform.Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview.Now Cuellar is one of several moderate Democrats angling to strike a deal with the White House, especially on reining in ICE officers and creating legal pathways to citizenship for some immigrants. They’re undeterred by President Donald Trump’s elevation of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff. And they’re buoyed by Trump’s recent admission that his deportations policy was “too tough.”Several of these Democrats have already placed calls to Trump and DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin to express a willingness to work together. Cuellar said he reached back out to Venturella and Scott after the election to try to schedule meetings.“If the president, as the president of the United States, makes a decision — and not a chief of staff — we can get the job done,” Cuellar said in an interview. “I’m sure we’re going to find a lot of differences, but if we sit down, we can definitely resolve them.”It’ll be a tough road: Securing buy-in from the White House becomes undoubtedly more complicated with Miller, a champion of the administration’s aggressive deportation push. Republicans in Congress have largely been willing to defer to the president on the issue. And Democratic leaders have questioned Trump’s sincerity and said they have no interest in working with Miller.The possibility will become even more tenuous once Democrats begin investigating the Trump administration, including the president’s immigration enforcement agencies.CBP and ICE did not respond to requests for comment.Neither did Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries.Democrats like Cuellar, Sen.-elects James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are aware of all of those hurdles. But they’re betting the midterms have created an opening for serious talks: Latino voters across the country swung hard back toward Democrats this cycle, and more and more Republicans are recognizing that their immigration agenda hurt them politically.Talarico and Andrews have publicly expressed interest in working with the president on immigration, and both ran on platforms that emphasized creating paths to citizenship for undocumented immigrants.“I’m ready to work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system,” Talarico said in a statement.Inside the White House, there’s a recognition that the president will proceed however he so chooses, regardless of who the chief of staff is. Trump is accessible to outside voices — journalists, business leaders and lawmakers regularly call him directly — and often poses policy questions to aides and allies as he decides which direction he will go.“Everybody’s like, ‘Well, it’s never going to happen with Stephen Miller.’ Look, Donald Trump’s the president. I don’t care if Stephen Miller’s the chief of staff or Susie Wiles or John Kelly or whoever the chief of staff might be,” said a person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak about the internal dynamic.For Democrats, there’s a real political incentive to getting a deal done ahead of a critical 2028 presidential election — especially as the party seeks to win back voter trust on immigration and border security, policy areas that spelled doom for them in 2024.“You have these Democrats who flip red states, and it’s also to their self-interest, right? Not just to do rhetoric, and go big or go home, but actually come to the middle with the president, with the Republicans. Because if not, I think that the big lesson this election is, Hispanic voters are gonna flip back ... if they don’t see Democrats delivering anything the next two years,” said Rebecca Shi, the executive director of ABIC, a coalition of pro-immigration reform business executives.She added that there’s a lesson for Republicans, too, if they don’t come to the table: “They will lose the White House.”White House spokesperson Lauren Bis touted Trump’s immigration accomplishments, including border security, a drop in crime and the creation of the Homeland Security Task Force and said the president’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.”She said Democrats should work alongside Trump to “keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.”Democrats welcomed the president’s remarks on 60 Minutes on Sunday, when he said he was open to legal pathways for some unauthorized immigrants who haven’t committed crimes and are working and contributing to the economy. Mullin also floated an openness to a bipartisan immigration overhaul involving DACA, which could provide permanent legal status to some undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, even as he — and the president — have insisted that any proposal wouldn’t include amnesty.In a sign that Democrats have learned the lessons of the Biden administration, many of them are eager to pair reforms with border security measures.Cuellar, who will chair the Homeland Security Appropriations subcommittee in the next conference, has long suggested including guardrails on ICE in the next funding bill, such as requiring judicial warrants, rolling out body camera usage and restoring “sensitive locations” such as churches and schools as off-limits.Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), another Democrat who has expressed interest in working with the Trump administration, said that beyond “talk,” it would help to see some smaller concrete policy shifts from the White House to affirm that Trump is, in fact, open to changes to the immigration system.“The way to do that is to have some reforms already at ICE — whether it’s shutting down these detention centers, giving certain level of protections, whether to veterans, so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. citizens, they don’t get deported — something to show that, you know, it's not just talk, this isn’t going to be a policy led by Stephen Miller,” he said.But Miller remains a bogeyman for Democrats, someone they view as responsible for the president’s most extreme immigration policies. As chief of staff, he can ensure he’s one of the last people in the president’s ear — and that the White House doesn’t bend to what he sees as unrealistic Democratic demands.“The reason why they wouldn’t do an amnesty deal, I believe, is because it would be the ultimate and most public contradiction of the central thesis of this entire political program as it was sold to voters,” said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project and a member of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “It would be the end of the America First coalition as it currently exists.”Democrats' distrust of Miller will also make it challenging for them to align on any potential deal with the White House.“Stephen Miller is the mastermind and architect of terror, and death, and illegality in this country, and he is not anyone who even understands truthfully what immigration policy should look like,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif).“No deals, man. No deals,” she added.The White House pointed to Miller’s experience on the Hill as a valuable asset. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said unlike Democrats “who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance.”Lawmakers are waiting for the president to make the first move.Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead his fellow Republicans when Democrats retake control of the Senate this January, told reporters after the election that “if there's something he wants to do there, we can have that conversation.”“There are always some landmines, which is why in the past the wheels have kind of come off, despite some really good efforts at trying to find a landing spot. But yeah we're open to something he wants to propose,” Thune added.Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

items.content: Protesters outside Shannon Airport, Co Clare, where President Donald Trump will depart from at the end of his trip to the Republic of Ireland, on Sept. 13, 2026. —Clodagh Kilcoyne—PA Images/Getty ImagesAn Irish man has been charged in the U.S. with wielding an axe and using chemicals to destroy an American military plane in what supporters have described as a protest against the U.S. military.Federal prosecutors in Manhattan accused 48-year-old Daithí O’Corrain of damaging a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard aircraft while it was parked at Ireland’s Shannon airport in April. O’Corrain allegedly cut hydraulic lines, smashed cockpit gauges, and poured ball bearings into the fuel tanks of the plane, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday.O’Corrain is not in U.S. custody and his arraignment has not been scheduled. He was arrested by Irish police after the April 11 incident. He faces one charge in the U.S. of destruction of government property, and three charges in Ireland of trespassing, causing criminal damage to the perimeter fence at the airport, and causing criminal damage to the plane. If convicted, the U.S. charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.“These charges send a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets—and thus our national security—will not be tolerated,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement.A group of public supporters has rallied around O’Corrain, characterizing his actions as a political protest against the U.S. war with Iran and military aid to Israel. An online fundraiser described him as an “independent peace activist” and called the incident “an inspiring act of direct action … to resist the unwanted presence of the U.S. Military in Ireland.” Anti-nuclear, anti-war newspaper The Nuclear Resister reported in August that activists attended his court hearings in Ireland. Social media accounts made in support of O’Corrain posted information about solidarity protests and argued that the aircraft’s presence violated Irish rules governing foreign military aircraft. The Irish government has said that U.S. military aircraft landing in Ireland are subject to conditions, including restrictions on carrying arms without permission, and that missions aren’t launched from the airport.O’Corrain has not made any public statements and is not known to be involved in any activist groups behind earlier protests at the airport, including when President Donald Trump visited in September.Here’s what to know about the charges.Prosecutors say O’Corrain planned for monthsAccording to the indictment, O’Corrain breached the airport’s security perimeter at around 4:39 a.m. local time and entered the aircraft by breaking its rear crew door’s locking mechanism. He then covered the plane’s windows, except those in the cockpit, barricaded himself inside, and placed ball bearings mixed with epoxy into the plane door tracks to block them from being opened, the indictment alleges.O’Corrain is alleged to have cut wire bundles and hydraulic lines, crimped a liquid oxygen line, destroyed the gauges in the cockpit, and punctured the plane’s air ducts. At around 9:40 a.m., the flight crew saw O’Corrain escaping out of a roof hatch before striking the plane with an axe and pouring unknown substances and ball bearings into the plane’s fuel tanks, according to the indictment.Handout photo of items allegedly used by Irish national Daithi O'Corrain to barricade himself in a U.S. military aircraft, distributed on Nov. 17, 2026. —U.S. Department of Justice/Press Association/APProsecutors alleged that O’Corrain had planned for months to break into the airport and damage the aircraft, including searching online about the construction of the C-130 Hercules aircraft and for coordinates for where to breach the airport’s security perimeter. The plane, a quad-engine turboprop that is mainly used for military transport, was parked on the airport’s taxiway while en route to a military assignment in another country.Prosecutors also alleged that O’Corrain ordered capsules of a corrosive chemical, gallium, online, subscribed to a flight-tracker app, and attempted to contact a person who had been arrested in connection with a prior breach at the airport. He demonstrated “detailed knowledge” of the layout of the aircraft and how to destroy its critical components without compromising his safety, the indictment said, adding that he knew in advance the aircraft would be there.“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” said James Barnacle, head of the FBI’s New York office.Anti-war protests at Shannon AirportShannon Airport has been the site of multiple protests against what critics describe as Ireland’s role in allowing U.S. military flights and troop transport through the airport. Protesters have argued that the U.S.’s involvement in various wars, particularly ongoing ones in Iran and Gaza, conflicts with Irish military neutrality.According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israel has killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel, which killed around 1,200 people in Israel and saw about 250 others taken hostage. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. An investigation by The Guardian estimated that 83% of Palestinians killed in Gaza were civilians as of May 2025, citing data from the Israel Defense Forces.In April 2017, Dan Dowling, then 35, and Edward Horgan, then 71, entered a restricted area and wrote “Danger, danger, do not fly” in red marker on a U.S. Navy aircraft. They were arrested in Ireland, and the jury heard in court that the markings were wiped off before the plane flew onward to a U.S. base in the Middle East.“If you want my motivation, it is the killing of children in Iraq, Syria, Afghanistan and Yemen,” Horgan told reporters at the time, calling their action an “informative protest” to highlight that U.S. military aircraft were not being searched. He said he had handed Irish police at the airport a 35-page-long list of 1,000 children killed in conflicts involving the U.S. in the Middle East, Asia, and Africa.Both men were acquitted of criminal damage in 2023, but convicted of trespass. Earlier this month, Ireland’s Supreme Court overturned Dowling’s trespass conviction. His attorney argued that the men believed their actions were necessary to protect lives.On March 10, 2024, pro-Palestinian activists held a sit-in inside the terminal calling for an end to U.S. weapons transfers through Ireland. Later that month, three pro-Palestinian activists approached a U.S. military aircraft carrying a Palestinian flag and a banner that read, “U.S. military out of Shannon.” They sat near the plane in an attempt to stop it from taking off. The activists were arrested and charged. Their trial was adjourned in February pending the Supreme Court ruling in Dowling’s appeal.Galway Palestine Solidarity Campaign organizer Rania Muhareb told Irish newspaper The Journal that the activists were protesting “in line with a long tradition of Irish anti-war activism at Shannon.”Around 500 people held another protest in support of Palestinians in April 2024 at the airport entrance, while a smaller group blocked the access road.In May 2025, three people were arrested for driving a van through the airport’s perimeter fence in what was reported as a pro-Palestinian protest. In a separate incident that month, three women allegedly entered the runway and spray-painted the nose of a plane of Omni Air, a civilian airline that transports U.S. military personnel. Irish broadcaster RTÉ reported that the plane was not engaged in military activity. The women were arrested and charged with criminal damage and trespass, which they denied.That November, three people were charged over allegedly entering the airfield and spray-painting a U.S. Navy Reserve Boeing 737 parked at Shannon. Their stated objection was that U.S. military use of Shannon violated Irish neutrality and supported Israel’s war in Gaza.Hundreds of protesters also gathered near Shannon Airport during President Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland in September, chanting “U.S. military out of Shannon.”

items.title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years in US prison over Trump murder plot
items.standfirst: Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani deathA Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
